SWE-bench Verified is the benchmark every coding-model launch quotes, and as of June 16, 2026 the headline is striking: Claude Fable 5 sits at the top of the llm-stats leaderboard with a reported 95.0%. The problem is what that number hides. Ninety-nine of the hundred entries on that board are self-reported, the same model family scores far lower on a standardized harness, and one of the labs that helped make the benchmark famous has quietly stopped reporting it at all.
This is not a story about which model is best. It is a story about why a single benchmark name now points to three or four genuinely different numbers — and why the agent scaffold around a model can move a score by 10 to 20 points without changing the model at all. For anyone choosing a coding model for real work, the rank order on a leaderboard is the least useful thing on the page.
Below we separate the four distinct measurements hiding behind “SWE-bench,” show where the vendor numbers and the standardized numbers diverge, explain the contamination problem that pushed OpenAI to walk away, and lay out how to read all of it when you actually have to pick a model. It builds on our broader [SWE-bench live leaderboard Q2 2026 analysis](https://www.digitalapplied.com/blog/swe-bench-live-leaderboard-q2-2026-analysis) with a sharper focus on the harness.
  1. 01
The headline rank is mostly self-reported.The llm-stats SWE-bench Verified leaderboard listed 100 models on June 16, 2026 — but only 1 result was independently verified; the other 99 were submitted by the vendors themselves. Fable 5's 95.0% is the rare independently-confirmed one (vals.ai).
  2. 02
One benchmark name, several different numbers.SWE-bench Verified (self-reported), SWE-bench Pro on a vendor scaffold, SWE-bench Pro on Scale's standardized SEAL harness, and SWE-bench Pro on a private commercial subset can all carry the same model and produce sharply different results.
  3. 03
The harness can be worth more than the model.Three different agent systems running the same Claude Opus 4.5 produced a 50.2%–55.4% range on SWE-bench Pro — a 5.2-point spread from scaffold differences alone. Scale's own analysis attributes 10–20 point swings to harness choices.
  4. 04
Vendor Pro scores sit well above standardized ones.Anthropic reports 69.2% for Opus 4.8 on SWE-bench Pro using its own scaffold, while the best Claude score on Scale's standardized SEAL board is 51.9% (Opus 4.6 thinking) — a 17.3-point gap within a single model family.
  5. 05
Buy on the standardized and private numbers, not the headline.For purchase decisions, treat SWE-bench Verified as a pass/fail tier filter and lean on SEAL-standardized SWE-bench Pro plus the private-codebase subset — the only numbers measured the same way for every model, on tasks closer to proprietary work.

passages.text:
# SWE-bench Verified
SWE-bench Verified
Methodology
### SWE-bench Verified
[SWE-bench Verified](https://openai.com/index/introducing-swe-bench-verified/) is a human-validated subset of the original [SWE-bench](https://www.swebench.com/) dataset, consisting of 500 samples that evaluate AI models’ ability to solve real-world software engineering issues. Epoch evaluations of this benchmark use 484 samples that are validated on our infrastructure. Each sample is derived from a GitHub issue in one of 12 open-source Python repositories. Our [review of SWE-bench Verified](https://epoch.ai/blog/what-skills-does-swe-bench-verified-evaluate) examines the benchmark in more detail.
The evaluation workflow is as follows: the model is given access to a code repository and a description of an issue that needs to be fixed. The model must then investigate and modify the repository to resolve the issue. Once the model has made its changes, the solution is evaluated by running unit tests on the modified codebase.
The dataset was curated through a rigorous human annotation process involving 93 software developers. Each sample was reviewed by three separate annotators to ensure the issue description is well-specified, the unit tests are appropriate, and the sample is free of other major issues that could make evaluation unreliable. Nevertheless, some samples may remain ambiguous – and we have previously estimated an [error rate of 5-10%](https://epoch.ai/blog/what-skills-does-swe-bench-verified-evaluate#the-error-rate-in-swe-bench-verified-is-relatively-low).
### Methodology
There are five parts to our SWE-bench Verified evaluation methodology:
  * Prompts and other information to direct the model.
  * Scaffold and tools used when running the model.
  * Samples used for evaluation.
  * Limits on model input/output.
  * Environment the benchmark runs in.

arXiv:2511.16858v2 [cs.SE] 27 Jan 2026
# Investigating Test Overfitting on SWE-bench
Toufique Ahmed, Jatin Ganhotra, Avraham Shinnar, and Martin Hirzel  Affiliation: IBM, Yorktown Heights, New York, USA, 10603 email: tfahmed@ibm.com, jatinganhotra, shinnar, hirzel@us.ibm.com
###### Abstract.
Tests can be useful towards resolving issues on code repositories. However, relying too much on tests for issue resolution can lead to code that technically passes observed tests but actually misses important cases or even breaks functionality. This problem, called _test overfitting_ , is exacerbated by the fact that issues usually lack readily executable tests. Instead, several issue resolution systems use tests auto-generated from issues, which may be imperfect. Some systems even iteratively refine code and tests jointly. This paper presents the first empirical study of test overfitting in this setting.
###### Keywords: 
LLMs, SWE Patches, Reproduction Tests 
##  1. Introduction
Issue resolution systems, which automatically resolve bug reports or feature requests in code repositories, are useful. They are also challenging to build, because issue descriptions tend to be informal and code repositories are often large and complex ([Jimenez et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.16858v2#bib.bib11)). Several issue resolution systems leverage tests: for code candidate selection in parallel inference scaling ([Arora et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.16858v2#bib.bib3); [Gao et al., 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.16858v2#bib.bib9); [Jain et al., 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.16858v2#bib.bib10); [Ruan et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.16858v2#bib.bib16); [Xia et al., 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.16858v2#bib.bib20); [Zhang et al., 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.16858v2#bib.bib23)), code refinement in sequential inference scaling ([Chen et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.16858v2#bib.bib6); [Li et al., 2025b](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.16858v2#bib.bib12); [Yang et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.16858v2#bib.bib21); [Zhang et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.16858v2#bib.bib22)), or both ([Ehrlich et al., 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.16858v2#bib.bib8); [Li et al., 2025c](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.16858v2#bib.bib13)). These systems rely upon the implicit premise that tests offer a reliable signal in this setting. Unfortunately, little is known about whether this premise holds. To the contrary, startling results in adjacent settings cast doubt upon it ([Baker et al., 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.16858v2#bib.bib4); [Smith et al., 2015](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.16858v2#bib.bib17); [Stroebl et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.16858v2#bib.bib18)). Relying upon tests for issue resolution can cause _test overfitting_ : generated code that narrowly passes the observed tests but breaks other functionality. This paper empirically investigates the problem of test overfitting in repository-level issue resolution, on benchmarks such as SWE-bench ([Jimenez et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.16858v2#bib.bib11)).
An issue resolution system takes an issue description dissued_{\textrm{issue}} along with the original code coldc_{\textrm{old}} of a repository as input and produces modified code cnewc_{\textrm{new}} as output. While many repositories come with regression tests told⊂coldt_{\textrm{old}}\subset c_{\textrm{old}}, those only test existing behavior, not the desired functionality of dissued_{\textrm{issue}}. Instead, issue resolution systems are evaluated by running acceptance tests tgoldt_{\textrm{gold}} on cnewc_{\textrm{new}}. In SWE-bench, tgoldt_{\textrm{gold}} is mined from issue-resolving pull requests ([Jimenez et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.16858v2#bib.bib11)). Since most open issues lack acceptance tests, tgoldt_{\textrm{gold}} is not yet available during issue resolution — neither in practice nor in the benchmark. Therefore, several issue resolution systems instead generate surrogate tests tgent_{\textrm{gen}}, based only on dissued_{\textrm{issue}} and coldc_{\textrm{old}}. Since generated tests tgent_{\textrm{gen}} are imperfect, over-relying on them risks test overfitting, where cnewc_{\textrm{new}} passes tgent_{\textrm{gen}} but fails the hidden tgoldt_{\textrm{gold}}.

Figure 1. Test overfitting example on django__django-12308.
Figure shows a concrete example. Based on the issue description dissued_{\textrm{issue}}, an issue resolution system generates initial new code cnewc_{\textrm{new}} and a reproduction test generator generates a test tgent_{\textrm{gen}}. However, cnewc_{\textrm{new}} fails on tgent_{\textrm{gen}}, triggering code refinement based on observed test tgent_{\textrm{gen}}. The refined code cnew′c^{\prime}_{\textrm{new}} passes tgent_{\textrm{gen}} but overfits to it, since it fails other cases covered by the hidden golden test tgoldt_{\textrm{gold}}.
This paper empirically investigates test overfitting in issue resolution using popular large-scale open-source repositories and issues. It was inspired by two earlier studies. The paper “Is the cure worse than the disease?” demonstrated that test overfitting is a serious problem. But unlike our paper, it predated large language models (LLMs) and focused on student projects. The “Inference scaling FLaws” ([Stroebl et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.16858v2#bib.bib18)) paper found test overfitting to be a limiting factor for inference scaling in LLM-based code generation. But unlike our paper, it did not study repository-level tasks, nor did it explore test-based code refinement. Overall, while these papers highlighted the problem in adjacent settings, to our knowledge, ours is the first to explore it in the setting of LLM-based issue resolution.
Our empirical study answers three research questions:
  * RQ1.
Do LLM-generated code patches cnewc_{\textrm{new}} overfit to tests tgent_{\textrm{gen}} generated using the same LLM?
  * RQ2.
How does refining code cnewc_{\textrm{new}} based on observed tests tgent_{\textrm{gen}} affect test overfitting?
  * RQ3.
If the hidden tests tgoldt_{\textrm{gold}} were revealed, would refining code based on them break other functionality?

passages.source_title: Investigating Test Overfitting on SWE-bench
passages.text:
This paper demonstrates that test overfitting is a clear problem in modern LLM-based issue resolution systems. And unfortunately, while attempts to mitigate this overfitting do work to some extent, they also reduce effectiveness on the original task of issue resolution. Even if golden tests were available, refining code to pass them can still break other functionality. Overall, we caution against over-reliance on tests during code generation and hope to inspire future work in reducing test overfitting.
##  2. Background and Related Work
Test overfitting happens when an system generates code that passes observed tests but fails held-out hidden tests . Test overfitting is similar to overfitting a model to its training data, where the model performs worse on held-out test data; but note that in this work, we use only pre-trained LLMs without fine-tuning. Instead, test overfitting means that generated code cnewc_{\textrm{new}} is too narrow to generalize to held-out tests tgoldt_{\textrm{gold}}. Stroebl et al. report that this happens when a loop repeatedly generates code for the HumanEval or MBPP benchmarks until finding code that passes observed tests ([Stroebl et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.16858v2#bib.bib18)). Unlike Stroebl et al., we experiment with repository-level benchmarks and we also explore test-based code refinement loops.
SWE-bench is a benchmark where the input comprises an issue description dissued_{\textrm{issue}} and the original code coldc_{\textrm{old}} of an entire repository before issue resolution and the output is repaired code cnewc_{\textrm{new}} ([Jimenez et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.16858v2#bib.bib11)). Solutions are evaluated on whether cnewc_{\textrm{new}} passes a held-out test set tgoldt_{\textrm{gold}}. To emulate the real-world situation where issues do not come with readily executable tests, the benchmark does not make those held-out tests available to the issue resolution system. SWE-bench Verified is a subset of 500 high-quality SWE-bench instances, targeted by most issue resolution systems ([Chowdhury et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.16858v2#bib.bib7)). SWT-bench ([Mündler et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.16858v2#bib.bib15)) and TDD-Bench Verified ([Ahmed et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.16858v2#bib.bib1)) are reproduction test benchmarks derived from SWE-bench and SWE-Bench Verified.
Several issue resolution systems leverage generated tests tgent_{\textrm{gen}}. CodeT generates many code candidates and many candidate tests, then uses a dual execution agreement to pick a single output code . Agentless generates up to 40 candidate codes for SWE-bench and generates a reproduction test, then uses the test to filter the candidate codes as part of code selection . S* , CodeMonkeys ([Ehrlich et al., 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.16858v2#bib.bib8)), and InfCode also generate both candidate codes and candidate tests, followed by a loop where the LLM improves the code based on the test and vice versa. These papers might suffer from test overfitting but do not study it.
Test overfitting is related to _reward hacking_ , where a reward is a reinforcement-learning (RL) objective, and a hack finds a loop-hole for improving the reward while circumventing its intention. CURE uses RL to co-evolve an LLM to generate both code and white-box tests, and might be susceptible to test overfitting and reward hacking . Baker et al. found that RL to improve frontier LLMs for repository-level coding tasks can cause the reward hack of disabling tests instead of improving code ([Baker et al., 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.16858v2#bib.bib4)).
##  3. Methodology
We assume a simple three-step pipeline for issue resolution.
  1. (1)
Run an off-the-shelf issue resolver (Agentless ) on dissued_{\textrm{issue}} and original code coldc_{\textrm{old}} to obtain initial candidate code cnewc_{\textrm{new}}.
  2. (2)
Run an off-the-shelf reproduction test generator (e-Otter++ ([Ahmed et al., 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.16858v2#bib.bib2))) on dissued_{\textrm{issue}} and coldc_{\textrm{old}} to obtain an initial candidate test tgent_{\textrm{gen}}.
  3. (3)
Run test-based code refinement (described below) on the initial cnewc_{\textrm{new}} and tgent_{\textrm{gen}} to obtain final candidate code cnew′c^{\prime}_{\textrm{new}}.

# Why AI Coding Agents Create More Technical Debt
AI coding agents promise to eliminate technical debt, but their output often lacks architectural foresight and embeds business logic blind spots, creating a more insidious and costly maintenance burden. This article deconstructs the hidden costs of AI-generated code.
THE ARCHITECTURAL BLIND SPOT
## The AI Coding Paradox: Faster Velocity, Heavier Debt
AI coding agents accelerate initial development but systematically generate technical debt through architectural shortcuts and hidden complexity.
**AI-generated code lacks architectural foresight**. Tools like GitHub Copilot and Amazon CodeWhisperer optimize for local syntax, not system-wide design. They produce functionally correct code that ignores **bounded contexts** and **separation of concerns** , creating a distributed monolith.
**Velocity creates compounding maintenance debt**. Each AI-assisted commit introduces **micro-entropy** —minor inconsistencies in error handling, logging, and dependency management. These patterns compound, making the codebase **brittle and opaque** to human engineers.
**Business logic becomes an embedded mystery**. AI agents cannot infer undocumented rules from legacy systems. During [automated code modernization](https://inferensys.com/en/blog/automated-code-modernization-and-tech-debt-reduction/), they discard **tribal knowledge** , baking incorrect assumptions into new services. This creates a **maintenance time bomb**.
**Evidence** : Systems built with AI agents exhibit a 300% increase in **circular dependencies** and a 40% higher rate of **vendor lock-in** to specific cloud services like Pinecone or proprietary SDKs, compared to human-designed systems.
WHY AGENTS CREATE DEBT
## The Three Pillars of AI-Generated Technical Debt
AI coding agents accelerate delivery but introduce systemic, long-term maintenance burdens through architectural blindness, context-free generation, and uninstrumented automation.
### The Architectural Blindness Problem
AI agents optimize for local correctness, not system-wide integrity. They generate code that works in isolation but creates distributed monoliths and hidden coupling.
  * **Generates anti-patterns** like tight coupling and god objects.
  * **Ignores bounded contexts** , leading to spaghetti microservices.
  * **Lacks foresight** for scalability, creating $10K+ monthly cloud cost overruns.

by Madhup Mishra
# GitHub Copilot: Productivity boost or DORA metrics disaster?
feature
Aug 6, 20246 mins
Imagine a world where [measuring developer productivity](https://www.cio.com/article/1255774/is-it-worth-measuring-software-developer-productivity-cios-weigh-in.html) is as straightforward as checking your fitness stats on a smartwatch. With AI programming assistants like [GitHub Copilot](https://www.infoworld.com/article/2270790/review-github-copilot-preview-gives-me-hope.html), this seems within reach. GitHub Copilot claims to turbocharge developer productivity with context-aware code completions and snippet generation. By leveraging AI to suggest entire lines or modules of code, GitHub Copilot aims to reduce manual coding efforts, equivalent to having a supercharged assistant that helps you code faster and focus on complex problem-solving.
Organizations have used DevOps Research and Assessment (DORA) metrics as a structured approach to evaluating their [software development](https://www.infoworld.com/article/2261746/how-to-measure-developer-productivity-and-how-not-to.html) and [devops](https://www.infoworld.com/article/3215275/what-is-devops-transforming-software-development.html) team performance. This data-driven approach enables teams to deliver software faster with greater reliability and improved system stability. By focusing on deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate, and mean time to restore (MTTR), teams gain invaluable insights into their workflows.
## AI impact on DORA metrics
Here’s the kicker—DORA metrics are not all sunshine and rainbows. Misusing them can lead to a narrow focus on quantity over quality. Developers might game the system just to improve their metrics, like students cramming for exams without truly understanding the material. This can create disparities, as developers working on modern [microservices](https://www.infoworld.com/article/3445043/what-are-microservices-your-next-software-architecture.html)-based applications will naturally shine in DORA metrics compared to those handling older, monolithic systems.
The advent of AI-generated code exacerbates this issue significantly. While tools like GitHub Copilot can boost productivity metrics, the results might not necessarily reflect better deployment practices or system stability. The auto-generated code could inflate productivity stats without genuinely improving development processes.
Despite their potential, AI coding assistants introduce new challenges. Besides concerns about developer skill atrophy and ethical issues surrounding the use of public code, experts predict a massive increase in QA and security issues in software production, directly impacting your [DORA metrics](https://www.cio.com/article/1255774/is-it-worth-measuring-software-developer-productivity-cios-weigh-in.html).
Trained on vast amounts of public code, AI coding assistants might inadvertently suggest snippets with bugs or vulnerabilities. Imagine the AI generating code that doesn’t properly sanitize user inputs, opening the door to SQL injection attacks. Additionally, the AI’s lack of project-specific context can lead to misaligned code with the unique business logic or architectural standards of a project, causing functionality issues discovered late in the development cycle or even in production.
There’s also the risk of developers becoming overly reliant on AI-generated code, leading to a lax attitude toward code review and testing. Subtle bugs and inefficiencies could slip through, increasing the likelihood of defects in production.
These issues can directly impact your DORA metrics. More defects due to AI-generated code can raise the change failure rate, negatively affecting deployment pipeline stability. Bugs reaching production can increase the mean time to restore (MTTR), as developers spend more time fixing issues caused by the AI. Additionally, the need for extra reviews and tests to catch errors introduced by AI assistants can slow down the development process, increasing the lead time for changes.
## Guidelines for development teams 
To mitigate these impacts, development teams must maintain rigorous code review practices and establish comprehensive testing strategies. These vast volumes of ever-growing AI-generated code should be tested as thoroughly as manually written code. Organizations must invest in end-to-end test automation and test management solutions to provide tracking and end-to-end visibility into code quality earlier in the cycle and systematically automate testing throughout. Development teams must manage the increased load of AI-generated code by becoming smarter about how they conduct code reviews, apply security tests, and automate their testing. This would ensure the continued delivery of high-quality software with the right level of trust. 
Here are some guidelines for software development teams to consider:
**Code reviews** — Incorporate testing best practices during code reviews to maintain code quality even with AI-generated code. AI assistants like GitHub Copilot can actually contribute to this process by suggesting improvements to test coverage, identifying areas where additional testing may be required, and highlighting potential edge cases that need to be addressed. This helps teams uphold high standards of code quality and reliability.
**Security reviews** — Treat every input in your code as a potential threat. To bolster your application against common threats like SQL injections or cross-site scripting (XSS) attacks that can creep in through AI-generated code, it’s essential to validate and sanitize all inputs rigorously. Create robust governance policies to protect sensitive data, such as personal information and credit card numbers, demanding additional layers of security.
**Automated testing** — Automate the creation of test cases, enabling teams to quickly generate steps for unit, functional, and integration tests. This will help manage the massive surge of AI-generated code in applications. Expand beyond just helping developers and traditional QA people by bringing in non-technical users to create and maintain those tests for automated end-to-end testing.
**API testing** — Using open specifications, create an AI-augmented testing approach for your APIs, including the creation and maintenance of API tests and contracts. Seamlessly integrate these API tests with developer tools to accelerate development, reduce costs, and maintain current tests with ongoing code changes.
**Better test management** — AI can help with intelligent decision-making, risk analysis, and optimizing the testing process. AI can analyze vast amounts of data to provide insights on test coverage, effectiveness, and areas that need attention.
While GitHub Copilot and other [AI coding assistants](https://www.csoonline.com/article/1311835/generative-ai-poised-to-make-substantial-impact-on-devsecops.html) promise a productivity boost, they raise serious concerns that could render DORA metrics unmanageable. Developer productivity might be superficially enhanced, but at what cost? The hidden effort in scrutinizing and correcting AI-generated code could overshadow any initial gains, leading to a potential disaster if not carefully managed. Armed with an approach that’s ready for AI-generated code, organizations must re-evaluate their DORA metrics to align better with AI-generated productivity. By setting the right expectations, teams can achieve new heights of productivity and efficiency.
_Madhup Mishra is senior vice president of product marketing at_[ _SmartBear_](https://smartbear.com/) _. With over two decades of technology experience at companies like Hitachi Vantara, Volt Active Data, HPE SimpliVity, Dell, and Dell-EMC, Madhup has held a variety of roles in product management, sales engineering, and product marketing. He has a passion for how artificial intelligence is changing the world._

reviewed_passages.text:
Serving tech enthusiasts for over 25 years. TechSpot means tech analysis and advice [you can trust](https://www.techspot.com/ethics.html). 
**In a nutshell:** Developers were supposed to be among the biggest beneficiaries of the generative AI hype as special tools made churning out code faster and easier. But according to a recent study from Uplevel, a firm that analyzes coding metrics, the productivity gains aren't materializing – at least not yet. 
The study tracked around 800 developers, [comparing](https://resources.uplevelteam.com/gen-ai-for-coding) their output with and without [GitHub's Copilot](https://www.techspot.com/news/104351-github-copilot-autofix-quickly-identifies-resolves-security-issues.html) coding assistant over three-month periods. Surprisingly, when measuring key metrics like pull request cycle time and throughput, Uplevel found no meaningful improvements for those using Copilot.
Matt Hoffman, a data analyst at Uplevel, [explained](https://www.cio.com/article/3540579/devs-gaining-little-if-anything-from-ai-coding-assistants.html) to the publication CIO that their team initially thought that developers would be able to write more code and the defect rate might actually go down because developers were using AI tools to help review code before submitting it. But their findings defied those expectations.
In fact, the study found that developers using Copilot introduced 41% more bugs into their code, according to CIO. Uplevel also saw no evidence that the AI assistant was helping prevent developer burnout.
The revelations counter claims from Copilot's makers at GitHub and other vocal AI coding tool proponents about massive productivity boosts. A GitHub-sponsored study earlier claimed developers wrote code 55% faster with Copilot's aid.
Developers could indeed be seeing positive results, given that a report from Copilot's early days [showed](https://www.techspot.com/news/91984-almost-30-percent-new-github-code-written-ai.html) nearly 30% of new code involved AI assistance – a number that has likely grown. However, another possibility behind the increase usage is coders developing a dependency and turning lazy.

# [Developers remain willing but reluctant to use AI: The 2025 Developer Survey results are here](https://stackoverflow.blog/2025/12/29/developers-remain-willing-but-reluctant-to-use-ai-the-2025-developer-survey-results-are-here/)
No need to bury the lede: more developers are using AI tools, but their trust in those tools is falling.

Ryan and Eira talk with Stack Overflow senior research analyst Erin Yepis about the results of our 2024 Developer Survey, which polled more than 65,000 developers about the tools they use, the technologies they want to learn, their experiences at work, and much more. Erin highlights what the survey reveals about devs’ favorite programming languages (JavaScript, HTML, Python), the rise of Rust, the popularity of embedded technologies (Raspberry Pi, Arduino), developer sentiment around AI, and why tech debt tops the list of developer frustrations.

reviewed_passages.text:
## What Is Devin AI and How Does It Work?
Devin is an AI software engineer built by Cognition AI, a startup that raised $21 million in seed funding and a subsequent $175 million Series A before its public launch. The product was announced in March 2024 with a demo video showing Devin independently solving a Upwork freelancing task and contributing to open-source repositories.
Unlike AI coding assistants that work inside your IDE — GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Claude Code — Devin operates as a fully autonomous coding agent. As an ai software engineer, it has its own shell environment, browser, and code editor. You give it a task in natural language, it plans the approach, executes across multiple steps, and comes back with results. This autonomy is the core differentiator. If you are new to this category, our [agentic AI tools explained](https://www.openaitoolshub.org/en/blog/agentic-ai-tools-explained) guide covers how these systems differ from standard chatbots and IDE assistants.
The marketing framing — "world's first fully autonomous AI software engineer" — generated significant skepticism from the engineering community. The SWE-Bench score of 13.86% was genuinely impressive at the time of announcement, but the benchmark measures a narrow slice of software engineering work. Real-world performance on diverse projects is considerably more mixed.
## How We Tested Devin
We ran Devin on three representative tasks over a three-week period:
  * **Task A (Bug Fix):** Reproduce and fix a race condition in a Node.js Express API that intermittently failed under concurrent requests. Codebase: ~3,000 lines.
  * **Task B (Feature Build):** Add a paginated search endpoint with full-text filtering to an existing PostgreSQL + FastAPI project from a written spec. Codebase: ~8,000 lines.
  * **Task C (Data Migration):** Write and execute a migration script to consolidate two legacy database tables into a new normalized schema, with rollback capability.

reviewed_passages.source_title: Investigating Test Overfitting on SWE-bench
reviewed_passages.text:
Our experiments use two LLMs, Claude-3.7 Sonnet and GPT-4o. We use strong existing LLM-based systems as a starting point, obtaining the candidate code cnewc_{\textrm{new}} from Agentless and the surrogate test tgent_{\textrm{gen}} from e-Otter++ ([Ahmed et al., 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.16858v2#bib.bib2)). We extend these systems with a test-based code refinement loop that is representative of those found in recent work ([Ehrlich et al., 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.16858v2#bib.bib8); [Li et al., 2025c](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.16858v2#bib.bib13); [Li et al., 2025b](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.16858v2#bib.bib12); [Li et al., 2025a](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.16858v2#bib.bib14)). The experiments are based on the TDD-bench Verified ([Ahmed et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.16858v2#bib.bib1)) benchmark for test-driven development, which is derived from SWE-bench ([Jimenez et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.16858v2#bib.bib11)). TDD-bench Verified comprises challenging real-world Python issue resolution tasks. This paper makes the following contributions.
  * •
It measures the degree of test overfitting by LLMs in repository-level issue resolution tasks.
  * •
It describes techniques to reduce overfitting and reports how they impact both overfitting and performance.
  * •
It also includes a limit study of how much an oracle with access to the hidden golden tests could help performance.

sections.markdown:
The earliest quantitative claim for AI coding assistance comes from GitHub, where developers using GitHub Copilot completed an identical programming task in an average of 1 hour 11 minutes versus 2 hours 41 minutes for developers without Copilot, a 55% faster completion rate [[150f02_p4]] [[5c047a_p0]]. The same body of work reported that between 60% and 75% of users felt more fulfilled and less frustrated, and that 73% reported staying in flow and 87% reported preserving mental effort on repetitive tasks [[150f02_p3]] [[150f02_p5]]. This framing presents productivity holistically, linking speed to satisfaction and reduced cognitive load, and it was positioned around typical tasks designed to reflect everyday development scenarios [[150f02_p1]] [[150f02_p2]]. The confidence interval for the speed gain was reported as 21% to 89% with statistical significance at P=.0017, indicating a wide range around the headline 55% figure even within the lab setting [[150f02_p4]] [[5c047a_p0]].

A directly contrasting result comes from METR, where experienced open-source developers working on real issues in their own mature repositories took 19% longer to complete tasks when allowed to use early-2025 AI tools [[91fbd2_p0]] [[2154b9_p1]]. The same developers estimated on average that AI had made them 20% faster, illustrating a divergence between perceived acceleration and measured completion time [[91fbd2_p0]]. METR itself labels this result as historical and not necessarily reflective of current tools or workflows, emphasizing that it is one study in a specific setting rather than settled consensus [[91fbd2_p0]]. The tension between the GitHub and METR results is not a simple contradiction to be resolved by choosing one number, but a signal that task type, codebase familiarity, and developer experience materially shape outcomes [[150f02_p4]] [[91fbd2_p0]].

Field data from Uplevel Data Labs, which examined 800 developers on large engineering teams before and after GitHub Copilot adoption with a test group with access and a control group without, found little to no productivity gain on delivery metrics such as pull request cycle time and throughput [[01298f_p1]] [[bfbda7_p0]]. That work also found that the group with Copilot access introduced 41% more bugs in pull requests while issue throughput remained consistent, suggesting a negative impact on code quality without a compensating speed gain [[bfbda7_p0]] [[f839b5_p0]]. A separate summary of the same research notes that Copilot access did not mitigate burnout risk, with the sustained-always-on metric decreasing by 17% for those with access versus 28% for those without [[01298f_p1]] [[bfbda7_p0]]. The implication is that even when individual task speed improves, the downstream costs of fixing defects and reviewing additional code can erase throughput gains at the team level [[01298f_p1]] [[bfbda7_p0]].

The DORA program, based on annual surveys of thousands of technology professionals, provides a broader organizational lens that helps reconcile these divergent findings [[1253eb_p0]] [[b67f42_p2]]. The 2024 DORA report found that a 25% increase in AI adoption was associated with a 7.5% increase in documentation quality, a 3.4% increase in code quality, and a 3.1% increase in code review speed, yet it also estimated a 1.5% decrease in delivery throughput and a 7.2% reduction in delivery stability as AI adoption increased [[1253eb_p0]] [[1253eb_p1]]. The report explicitly states that improving the development process does not automatically improve software delivery without adherence to fundamentals like small batch sizes and robust testing mechanisms [[1253eb_p1]]. By 2025, DORA reported that AI adoption had surged to 90% with a median of two hours daily spent with AI, and that over 80% of respondents indicated productivity gains and 59% reported positive influence on code quality, while also finding that AI amplifies existing organizational strengths and weaknesses rather than fixing struggling teams [[b67f42_p2]] [[dac982_p0]].

| Study | Setting | Measure | Result | Citation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| GitHub Copilot lab experiment | 95 professional developers, identical tasks | Task completion time | 55% faster with Copilot, 71 min vs 161 min, P=.0017 | [[150f02_p4]] |
| METR early-2025 | 16 experienced OSS developers, 246 real issues in own repos | Measured completion time | 19% slower with AI, yet 20% faster perceived | [[91fbd2_p0]] |
| Uplevel field study | 800 developers, pre/post Copilot, test vs control | PR cycle time, throughput, bug rate | No meaningful improvement, 41% more bugs | [[bfbda7_p0]] |
| DORA 2024 survey | Cross-industry survey | Delivery throughput and stability | -1.5% throughput, -7.2% stability with higher AI adoption | [[1253eb_p1]] |

Taken together, the evidence suggests that speed gains are most robust in short, well-specified, repetitive tasks in controlled environments, while complex, repository-specific work with experienced developers shows no gain or a net slowdown once review and debugging are included [[150f02_p4]] [[91fbd2_p0]] [[01298f_p1]]. The convergence between METR and Uplevel on the gap between perception and measurement, and between DORA 2024 and Uplevel on the lack of delivery-level improvement, contrasts with the convergence between GitHub's lab result and DORA 2025's self-reported productivity gains, highlighting that self-report and satisfaction do not reliably predict throughput [[91fbd2_p0]] [[bfbda7_p0]] [[b67f42_p2]]. For engineering leaders, the practical implication is that productivity should be assessed at the delivery system level, not the individual suggestion level, and that gains in documentation quality and review speed do not automatically translate into faster, more stable releases [[1253eb_p1]] [[1253eb_p0]].

The divergence also reflects differences in what is being measured, as GitHub's lab task isolates coding time on a greenfield-style problem, while METR and Uplevel capture the full cycle of understanding context, integrating changes, and fixing introduced defects in existing codebases [[150f02_p4]] [[91fbd2_p0]] [[bfbda7_p0]]. DORA's finding that AI adoption is associated with higher code review speed but lower delivery stability suggests that faster generation can create a bottleneck downstream if review capacity and test coverage do not scale accordingly [[1253eb_p0]] [[1253eb_p1]]. This helps explain why developers can feel more productive and satisfied while delivery metrics remain flat, as the cognitive relief of offloading boilerplate is real but does not necessarily reduce the total work required to ship safe, maintainable code [[150f02_p3]] [[150f02_p5]] [[01298f_p1]].
sections.title: Productivity: from lab acceleration to field stagnation

sections.markdown:
SWE-bench has become the primary measure of whether a coding agent can do real engineering work, by tasking models to resolve real GitHub issues across 12 popular Python repositories and verifying patches against existing test suites [[32f395_p0]] [[68e580_p0]]. The benchmark requires understanding and coordinating changes across multiple functions, classes, and files, interacting with execution environments, and processing long contexts [[0f13e9_p1]]. Because the original dataset contains noisy and underspecified instances, OpenAI and Princeton curated SWE-bench Verified, a human-validated subset of 500 instances where annotators reviewed problem descriptions, test patches, and solvability [[05b864_p0]] [[ac1d47_p0]]. Even this curated subset is evaluated by applying the test patch and generated patch to the buggy repository and checking whether modified test files pass, a validation process that is intentionally narrow [[85fbf9_p1]].

The limitation of that validation is central to reliability claims, as testing is rarely exhaustive and a patch may pass the relevant tests while failing to match developer expectations [[85fbf9_p0]] [[0c8636_p0]]. An empirical study of plausible patches on SWE-bench Verified introduced a differential patch testing technique, PatchDiff, to generate tests that reveal behavioral differences between generated and human-written ground-truth patches, finding that evaluations suffer from plausible but incorrect patches that inflate resolution rates [[85fbf9_p0]] [[0c8636_p0]]. A separate investigation of test overfitting on SWE-bench found that LLM-generated code patches can overfit to auto-generated reproduction tests, and that refining code to pass observed tests can break other functionality, with mitigation attempts reducing both overfitting and overall effectiveness [[b4c964_p0]] [[b4c964_p2]]. The evidence suggests that passing the benchmark's tests is a necessary but not sufficient condition for correctness, and that reported pass rates should be interpreted as an upper bound on true issue resolution [[85fbf9_p0]] [[b4c964_p2]].

Complementary work on test generation, SWT-Bench, proposes a benchmark based on popular GitHub repositories with real-world issues, ground-truth patches, and golden tests, and finds that code agents designed for repair can outperform systems designed specifically for test generation at formalizing issues into test cases [[5c4024_p0]] [[a96e69_p0]]. Generated tests are shown to be an effective filter for proposed fixes, doubling the precision of SWE-Agent in that study, which underscores that test quality is both a capability and a bottleneck for autonomous repair [[5c4024_p0]]. The finding that repair-oriented agents can generate relevant tests surprisingly well indicates that the same models that produce fixes can also help validate them, but also that the quality of that validation depends heavily on the agent's ability to understand the issue beyond the existing test suite [[5c4024_p0]] [[a96e69_p0]].

Reported capability levels have risen rapidly on these benchmarks, which itself creates interpretation risk [[e1a7ba_p0]] [[68e580_p0]]. One synthesis reports SWE-bench Verified climbing from 13% in early 2024 to 78% in May 2026, with top agents reaching 74-78% and TerminalBench top scores at 52-58%, while estimating real-world pull-request pass rates at 35-50% for top agents due to implicit conventions and reviewer expectations that benchmarks miss [[e1a7ba_p0]]. Another analysis notes that as of June 2026, Claude Fable 5 tops SWE-bench Verified at a reported 95.0%, but that 99 of 100 leaderboard entries are self-reported and that standardized harnesses show materially lower scores [[777741_p0]]. The gap between benchmark saturation and production acceptance suggests that headline pass rates overstate readiness for autonomous deployment without human review [[e1a7ba_p0]] [[777741_p0]]. The evidence also indicates that open-weight backed agents trail frontier closed-API agents by 25-40% on SWE-bench Verified, and that median time to PR for autonomous agents on medium-complexity tasks is 8-25 minutes, while ambient pair-programming agents show median time to acceptance of 30-90 seconds per suggestion [[e1a7ba_p0]].

The reliability picture is further complicated by the fact that SWE-bench Verified's human validation, while rigorous, still leaves an estimated error rate of 5-10% due to ambiguous samples, and that infrastructure incompatibilities lead independent evaluators to exclude some samples from re-runs [[234fd4_p0]] [[ef4eca_p0]]. This means that even the most careful benchmark cannot fully capture the implicit requirements, style conventions, and system-wide invariants that human reviewers enforce in production, which helps explain why real-world acceptance rates lag benchmark scores by 20 to 40 points [[e1a7ba_p0]] [[777741_p0]]. For teams considering autonomous agents, the implication is that benchmark performance should be treated as a tier filter for capability, not as a predictor of merge rate without additional investment in review and testing [[777741_p0]] [[e1a7ba_p0]].
sections.title: Reliability and correctness: what benchmarks measure and miss

sections.markdown:
Security evidence converges from user studies and large-scale model evaluations that AI-generated code frequently introduces vulnerabilities [[66ce65_p0]] [[834012_p0]]. A Stanford-led user study with 47 participants solving five security-related tasks across Python, JavaScript, and C found that participants with access to an AI assistant based on codex-davinci-002 wrote significantly less secure code than those without access, and were more likely to believe they had written secure code [[66ce65_p1]] [[d3d3ad_p0]]. The study found insecure solutions more often for four of five tasks when AI was available, and that participants who trusted the AI less and engaged more with prompt phrasing and parameter adjustment produced fewer vulnerabilities [[66ce65_p1]].

Large-scale testing reinforces the pattern across models and languages, with Veracode's 2025 GenAI Code Security Report evaluating 80 curated coding tasks across more than 100 large language models and finding that AI-generated code introduced security vulnerabilities in 45% of cases [[834012_p0]] [[28cae9_p0]]. The same report found that when given a choice between secure and insecure methods, models chose the insecure option 45% of the time, and that 45% of test cases introduced OWASP Top 10 vulnerabilities [[834012_p0]] [[b6cf2c_p0]]. Language-specific failure rates were highest for Java at 72% and significant for Python at 38%, JavaScript at 43%, and C# at 45% [[28cae9_p0]] [[0dd3cb_p0]]. Specific weakness categories showed even higher failure rates, with cross-site scripting at 86% and log injection at 88% [[834012_p0]].

An October 2025 update using the same 80-task benchmark found that most providers showed no meaningful improvement between July and October 2025, with Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.5 at 50% and Claude Opus 4.1 at 49%, while OpenAI's GPT-5 reasoning models achieved 72% for GPT-5 Mini and 70% for GPT-5, the first substantial jump recorded, attributed to internal reasoning similar to code review [[aeb7e5_p0]]. The report notes that larger, newer models did not generally improve security, and that the state of AI-generated code security shows no signs of improvement over time without explicit security requirements [[3a1637_p0]] [[0dd3cb_p0]]. The finding that reasoning models can improve security pass rates by 10 to 20 points suggests that additional inference-time deliberation can catch insecure patterns, but also that this improvement is currently isolated to one provider and does not reflect a broad industry trend [[aeb7e5_p0]] [[0dd3cb_p0]].

| Finding | Scale | Result | Citation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| User study insecure code | 47 participants, 5 tasks, 3 languages | AI-assisted participants wrote less secure code, overestimated security | [[66ce65_p1]] |
| Veracode 2025 large-scale | 80 tasks, 100+ LLMs, 4 languages | 45% of samples introduced vulnerabilities, 45% chose insecure method | [[834012_p0]] |
| Language risk | Same benchmark | Java 72% failure, Python 38%, JavaScript 43%, C# 45% | [[28cae9_p0]] |
| CWE-specific | Same benchmark | XSS 86% failure, log injection 88% failure | [[834012_p0]] |
| Model update Oct 2025 | Same 80 tasks | GPT-5 Mini 72% pass, most other providers flat or down | [[aeb7e5_p0]] |

The security findings help explain production adoption patterns, where developers report using tools they do not trust to produce secure output [[61d060_p0]] [[1253eb_p1]]. The DORA 2024 report found that 39% of respondents reported little to no trust in AI-generated code despite productivity gains, indicating a need to manage integration more thoughtfully [[1253eb_p1]]. Veracode's analysis frames the risk as amplified by vibe coding, where developers rely on AI without explicitly defining security requirements, and notes that AI also enables attackers to identify and exploit vulnerabilities more efficiently [[3a1637_p0]] [[b6cf2c_p0]]. The convergence between the Stanford user study and Veracode's large-scale testing on the 45% vulnerability rate, and between DORA and Stack Overflow on low trust, suggests that the security cost is not an edge case but a central characteristic of current AI-generated code that must be addressed through explicit prompting, automated scanning, and review processes [[66ce65_p1]] [[834012_p0]] [[61d060_p0]].

The implications for production are material, as the same tools that accelerate generation also increase the volume of code that must be reviewed for security, and the vulnerabilities introduced are often in high-severity categories that are difficult to detect without specialized scanning [[834012_p0]] [[39cb30_p0]]. Veracode's guidance emphasizes embedding security in agentic workflows, using software composition analysis, and providing real-time feedback in IDEs, reflecting that the security gap cannot be closed by model improvements alone but requires changes to how AI-generated code is produced and validated [[3a1637_p0]] [[39cb30_p3]]. The fact that participants who engaged more deeply with prompt phrasing and provided more context produced more secure code suggests that developer skill in directing AI is a meaningful mitigator, but also that this skill is not uniformly distributed and adds to the verification burden [[66ce65_p1]].
sections.title: Security: insecure code at scale and the trust deficit

sections.markdown:
Adoption metrics show near-universal exposure, with the Stack Overflow 2025 Developer Survey of 49,009 responses from 166 countries reporting 84% of developers now use or plan to use AI coding tools, up from 76% in 2024 and 70% in 2023 [[61d060_p0]] [[649b33_p0]]. Heavy reliance is also rising, with DORA 2025 reporting 90% adoption and a median of two hours daily working with AI, and 65% heavily relying on AI for software development [[b67f42_p2]]. Yet trust has moved in the opposite direction, with trust in AI accuracy dropping from 43% in 2024 to 33% in 2025, with 46% actively distrusting AI tools and only 3% highly trusting AI outputs [[61d060_p0]] [[499528_p0]]. AI favorability fell from 77% in 2023 to 72% in 2024 and then to 60% in 2025, with the erosion rate doubling in one year [[61d060_p0]].

The survey data also clarifies where AI is actually used in workflows, with developers reporting that AI handles research and documentation better than complex tasks, and that only around 4% believe AI truly excels at complexity while 29% say it struggles with complex tasks [[499528_p0]]. Early-career developers with 1-5 years of experience are the most enthusiastic daily users, while seasoned developers report the lowest high trust and highest high distrust, suggesting that expertise increases skepticism about output quality [[499528_p0]] [[61d060_p0]]. This aligns with the finding that AI coding agents are described as evolving from code completion to chat assistants to autonomous agents that plan, execute, debug, and test, with claimed potential to improve productivity by 2x to 3x, a claim that field data does not consistently support [[a3ce11_p0]] [[01298f_p1]].

Production deployment context further tempers benchmark optimism, with one 2026 synthesis estimating median time to PR for autonomous agents at 8-25 minutes for medium-complexity tasks and 30-90 seconds per suggestion for ambient pair-programming agents, while noting that open-weight backed agents trail frontier closed-API agents by 25-40% on SWE-bench Verified [[e1a7ba_p0]]. The same analysis emphasizes that real-world pull-request pass rates are materially below benchmark scores because benchmarks miss implicit conventions and reviewer expectations [[e1a7ba_p0]]. The evidence suggests that the most common production use remains partial assistance—research, documentation, and code explanation—rather than fully autonomous feature development, and that heavy users are more likely to use AI for understanding codebases and debugging than for writing entire features [[499528_p0]] [[61d060_p0]].

The trust crisis has direct implications for workflow design, as developers report using tools they fundamentally do not believe in, creating a 51-point gap between usage at 84% and trust at 33% [[61d060_p0]]. This gap is described as market dysfunction, where pressure to use AI coexists with skepticism about its output, and where the people who know code best are most skeptical, signaling a quality issue rather than a perception issue [[61d060_p0]] [[499528_p0]]. The DORA finding that 39% of respondents have little to no trust in AI-generated code, even as more than one-third report moderate to extreme productivity increases, reinforces that productivity and trust are not moving together and that managing AI integration requires explicit guidelines and open communication about its impact [[1253eb_p1]] [[1253eb_p0]].
sections.title: Production adoption: high usage, low trust, and workflow reality

sections.markdown:
Economic assessment is framed by DORA's ROI of AI-assisted Software Development report, which provides a practical framework for translating engineering metrics into business value and is positioned as a follow-up to the 2025 State of AI-assisted Software Development report [[020419_p1]] [[dfc47a_p1]]. The report's central argument is that AI acts as an amplifier, with the greatest returns coming not from tools themselves but from the quality of internal platforms, clarity of workflows, and alignment of teams, and that without this foundation AI creates localized pockets of productivity lost in downstream chaos [[020419_p1]] [[dac982_p0]]. This directly echoes the 2025 finding that strong teams become better with AI while struggling teams see existing problems intensified [[dac982_p0]] [[dac982_p1]].

A key concept in the ROI framework is the J-curve of value realization, where most organizations experience a temporary productivity dip before long-term gains, driven by three causes: the learning curve as teams adapt workflows, the verification tax imposed by reviewing AI-generated code, and the need to adapt downstream practices [[020419_p1]]. The verification tax is material because AI-generated code requires human review to catch the higher bug rates and security flaws documented in field and lab studies, and because review time itself was only modestly improved in DORA 2024 at 3.1% for a 25% adoption increase [[1253eb_p0]] [[bfbda7_p0]] [[834012_p0]]. Guidance for ROI measurement recommends making DORA metrics the north star and tracking AI-specific signals as leading indicators, rather than relying on lines of code, raw PR counts, or commits as business KPIs [[6fc1ef_p2]] [[6fc1ef_p3]].

Maintenance burden adds a longer-term cost dimension that is not captured in short-term speed metrics, with analysis of AI-generated code noting a 300% increase in circular dependencies and a 40% higher rate of certain maintenance issues, alongside architectural shortcuts that create distributed monoliths and hidden coupling [[829d58_p0]]. The same analysis describes velocity creating compounding micro-entropy in error handling, logging, and dependency management, making codebases brittle and opaque, and notes that AI agents cannot infer undocumented business logic, baking incorrect assumptions into new services [[829d58_p0]]. While these specific percentages come from a vendor-leaning analysis and should be treated as attributed claims rather than independent measurements, they align directionally with the DORA finding that AI magnifies existing technical and process weaknesses [[829d58_p0]] [[dac982_p0]]. The evidence suggests that each AI-assisted commit can introduce minor inconsistencies that compound over time, creating a maintenance burden that is more insidious than immediate defects because it degrades architectural integrity [[829d58_p0]].

Pricing and cost predictability further complicate ROI, with Devin cited as an example where entry pricing is advertised at $20 per month but usage-based Agent Compute Unit billing can lead to solo-developer bills of $150 to $250 or more for moderate use, with credits spent on failed tasks not refunded [[e956c1_p1]] [[e3752c_p6]]. This creates a gap between advertised entry price and realized cost that must be modeled against the verification and rework costs identified in the J-curve [[020419_p1]] [[e956c1_p1]]. The DORA ROI framework emphasizes that teams should baseline DORA metrics before piloting, shrink pull requests, and add automation, and that if a pilot does not move lead time or deployment frequency, the bottleneck likely lies in reviews, QA, or release cadence rather than code generation speed [[6fc1ef_p3]] [[020419_p1]]. The evidence suggests that organizations that treat AI as a platform change—updating reviews, automating checks, retraining onboarding, and measuring with DORA and SPACE—are more likely to capture value than those that treat it as a faster keyboard [[6fc1ef_p3]] [[dac982_p1]].

The economic picture is also shaped by the finding that AI adoption is associated with improvements in documentation quality and code review speed, but that these gains do not automatically translate into financial return without strong version control practices, small batches, and healthy data ecosystems [[1253eb_p0]] [[2fdb52_p1]]. DORA's AI Capabilities Model identifies seven capabilities that magnify AI's positive impact, including user-centric focus, strong version control, AI-accessible internal data, and quality internal platforms, indicating that ROI depends on a system of practices rather than a single tool [[2fdb52_p1]] [[dac982_p1]]. The evidence suggests that the initial productivity dip is not a sign of failure but an expected phase that must be planned for, and that defending budget for AI requires conversation starters that link engineering metrics to business value through this broader system lens [[dfc47a_p1]] [[020419_p1]].
sections.title: Economics and ROI: the J-curve, verification tax, and maintenance burden

sections.markdown:
Vendor claims and independent measurements diverge systematically across productivity and capability benchmarks [[f73ce3_p0]] [[777741_p0]]. On productivity, GitHub's reported 55% faster completion and high satisfaction are vendor-led findings from a controlled experiment, while independent or field-oriented studies from METR and Uplevel find slower completion, no throughput gain, and higher bug rates, with DORA's independent survey research finding negative delivery impacts in 2024 before a more positive but conditional relationship in 2025 [[150f02_p4]] [[91fbd2_p0]] [[bfbda7_p0]] [[1253eb_p1]].

On capability benchmarks, the gap is quantified through independent re-runs under standardized conditions [[f73ce3_p0]] [[ef4eca_p0]]. Epoch AI, which independently re-runs SWE-bench Verified on 484 of 500 samples using fixed token limits, consistent scaffolding, and standardized Docker environments, found that DeepSeek's self-reported 57.6% with an Agentless scaffold measured 33% under standardized conditions, a 24-point gap [[f73ce3_p0]]. Epoch also reports that after methodology updates, most models now score close to vendor claims, but that GPT-5.1 scored 68% in their scaffold versus 76.3% reported by OpenAI, while GPT-5.2 scored 74%, indicating persistent variance even after improvements [[ef4eca_p0]]. A separate analysis of SWE-bench Verified as of June 2026 notes that 99 of 100 leaderboard entries are self-reported, that Claude Fable 5 is reported at 95.0% on the vendor leaderboard, and that the same model family scores 51.9% on Scale's standardized SEAL board versus 69.2% vendor-reported on SWE-bench Pro, a 17.3-point gap within a single family [[777741_p0]].

Historical vendor claims illustrate the methodology mismatch problem, with Cognition reporting Devin at 13.86% on SWE-bench by evaluating on a randomly chosen 25% subsample of 570 of 2,294 issues, compared to baselines computed on the full dataset, and choosing the stronger assisted baseline numbers for comparison [[f77782_p2]] [[e3752c_p6]]. Independent real-world testing cited in a 2026 review found only 3 of 20 tasks succeeding in an Answer.AI study, with 14 failures and unpredictability about which tasks would work, contrasting with Cognition's own metrics showing improving PR-merge rates [[e956c1_p0]] [[e956c1_p1]]. The review also notes that all benchmark figures for newer Cognition models are company-reported and that independent verification on contamination-resistant evaluations is the standard before treating them as settled [[9c64af_p2]].

The accountability gap is structural, as benchmark submission is voluntary, self-reported, and unaudited, with no third party required to sign off before a number reaches the leaderboard, though Princeton now flags self-reported scores and Scale AI created SEAL as an independently-run alternative [[def2ec_p1]] [[f73ce3_p0]]. OpenAI's decision to stop reporting SWE-bench Verified after discovering training-data contamination across frontier models is cited as a signal that the self-reporting era is ending, with enterprise buyers increasingly expected to demand verified scores as a procurement requirement [[def2ec_p1]] [[777741_p0]]. The evidence suggests that the same model can show a 10 to 20 point spread depending on the harness, and that the number that sells a model and the number that predicts results in a buyer's environment are rarely the same [[777741_p0]] [[f73ce3_p0]].

| Comparison | Vendor-reported | Independent standardized | Gap | Citation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| DeepSeek SWE-bench Verified | 57.6% Agentless scaffold | 33% Epoch AI standardized | 24 points | [[f73ce3_p0]] |
| GPT-5.1 SWE-bench Verified | 76.3% OpenAI | 68% Epoch AI scaffold | 8.3 points | [[ef4eca_p0]] |
| Claude Opus SWE-bench Pro | 69.2% Anthropic scaffold | 51.9% SEAL standardized | 17.3 points | [[777741_p0]] |
| Devin SWE-bench | 13.86% on 25% subsample | Baselines on full dataset | Not directly comparable | [[f77782_p2]] |

Taken together, the evidence suggests that vendor-reported benchmark scores should be treated as attributed claims reflecting optimal scaffolding and prompting, while independent standardized evaluations provide the more conservative estimate of expected performance in a buyer's environment [[def2ec_p1]] [[777741_p0]] [[f73ce3_p0]]. The finding that Epoch's updated tools and prompt improvements closed much of the gap for most models indicates that scaffolding quality is a major driver of variance, but also that this variance is not random noise but a systematic effect that can be exploited to inflate headline numbers [[ef4eca_p0]] [[777741_p0]]. For procurement, the implication is to treat SWE-bench Verified as a pass/fail tier filter and to lean on standardized and private-codebase evaluations for purchase decisions, as these are measured the same way for every model and closer to proprietary work [[777741_p0]].
sections.title: Vendor claims versus independent evidence: the benchmark credibility gap

sections.markdown:
The strongest supportable conclusion is that AI coding agents deliver measurable value in specific, well-scoped tasks such as boilerplate generation, documentation, and code explanation, where lab studies and self-reported satisfaction converge, but that this value does not reliably translate into faster delivery, higher quality, or more secure code at the team or organization level without substantial process investment [[150f02_p4]] [[150f02_p3]] [[1253eb_p0]]. Independent field studies and the DORA program converge on the finding that throughput and stability can stagnate or decline when AI adoption outpaces testing, review, and platform maturity, while security studies converge on a 45% vulnerability introduction rate and a trust deficit that widens as adoption grows [[bfbda7_p0]] [[1253eb_p1]] [[834012_p0]] [[61d060_p0]]. Reliability claims based on SWE-bench are inflated by test incompleteness and self-reported scaffolding effects, with independent audits documenting 15-35 point gaps and meaningful false-positive rates that must be discounted when projecting production performance [[f73ce3_p0]] [[777741_p0]] [[85fbf9_p0]].

The largest uncertainty is the net economic effect after accounting for the verification tax, rework from higher bug and vulnerability rates, and long-term maintenance burden from architectural shortcuts, all of which are poorly quantified in vendor ROI narratives but central to DORA's J-curve framework [[020419_p1]] [[829d58_p0]] [[bfbda7_p0]]. Current evidence does not provide a quantitative framework that reliably converts benchmark pass rates or lab speed gains into delivery throughput, change failure rate, or mean time to restore at scale, and the available ROI guidance explicitly warns that gains are conditional on platform quality, small batches, and healthy data ecosystems [[2fdb52_p1]] [[6fc1ef_p2]] [[dac982_p1]]. The evidence also leaves open how quickly the security gap can be closed, as the only substantial improvement observed comes from one provider's reasoning models, while most other providers show no progress over the same period [[aeb7e5_p0]] [[0dd3cb_p0]].

The assessment would change with three types of evidence that are currently missing or limited: longitudinal, team-level trials that measure DORA metrics, defect escape rates, and security incidents over multiple release cycles rather than single tasks; independent, contamination-resistant, standardized evaluations of agents on private codebases with reviewer acceptance as the outcome, rather than test-suite pass rates alone; and published, audited cost data linking AI usage, review time, rework, and incident remediation to financial return, including the J-curve dip duration and magnitude [[020419_p1]] [[e1a7ba_p0]] [[def2ec_p1]]. Until such evidence is available, the prudent interpretation is that AI coding agents are best treated as accelerators for well-instrumented teams with strong review and testing discipline, not as autonomous substitutes for engineering judgment, and that procurement and adoption decisions should weight independent standardized scores and field defect data more heavily than vendor-reported speed and benchmark headlines [[6fc1ef_p3]] [[dac982_p0]] [[777741_p0]]. The evidence suggests that the gap between announcements and production reality is not a temporary lag but a structural feature of how AI coding agents are currently built, measured, and deployed, and that closing it requires investment in the surrounding system of work rather than in the model alone [[dac982_p0]] [[020419_p1]] [[1253eb_p1]].
sections.title: Synthesis: what the evidence supports and what would change the assessment

events.summary:
AI coding agents in production show a consistent pattern of strong adoption paired with uneven evidence on outcomes, where measured productivity, reliability and security results diverge sharply from marketing claims [[61d060_p0]] [[91fbd2_p0]] [[834012_p0]]. Controlled lab studies have reported large speed gains for AI-assisted developers, while trials on experienced developers working in their own mature repositories and large-scale field studies have found no throughput gain, slower completion, and higher defect rates [[150f02_p4]] [[91fbd2_p0]] [[bfbda7_p0]]. Security evaluations at both user-study and large-scale model-testing scale find that AI assistance increases insecure code and that nearly half of AI-generated code samples introduce vulnerabilities, with trust in AI output falling even as usage rises [[66ce65_p1]] [[834012_p0]] [[61d060_p0]].

Reliability assessment is constrained by benchmark design, where the most cited measure of real-world issue resolution, SWE-bench Verified, relies on existing repository tests that can accept plausible but incorrect patches, and where independent re-evaluation has documented meaningful false-positive rates [[05b864_p0]] [[85fbf9_p0]]. Vendor-reported scores on this benchmark are systematically higher than independent standardized re-runs, with gaps of 15 to 35 points documented across model families and scaffolds, and with early high-profile claims based on subsampled evaluations that are not directly comparable to full-dataset baselines [[f73ce3_p0]] [[777741_p0]] [[f77782_p2]]. The DORA research program finds that AI adoption alone does not improve delivery performance and can reduce throughput and stability without strong underlying engineering practices, framing AI as an amplifier of existing strengths and weaknesses rather than a standalone fix [[1253eb_p1]] [[dac982_p0]].

Taken together, the evidence suggests that productivity benefits are task- and context-dependent, that reliability and security costs are material and often underestimated in vendor narratives, and that economic return depends on managing a verification tax and an initial productivity dip through platform quality, small batches, and robust testing [[020419_p1]] [[1253eb_p1]] [[829d58_p0]]. The decisive uncertainty is not whether agents can generate functional code quickly in isolated tasks, but whether organizations can absorb the review, testing, and maintenance burden required to make that code safe and maintainable at scale [[020419_p1]] [[66ce65_p1]] [[85fbf9_p0]].

You are the lead researcher directing a long-horizon research investigation. Each turn you see the question, your own brief, the evidence admitted so far, and a live budget line; you decide what to search next, when to pivot, and when the evidence is sufficient for the report to be written.

METHOD:
- FIRST TURN: map the question top-down before narrowing. In the brief, name the major angles a domain expert would expect; put the angles that still need evidence in coverage.open. This is a living map, not a fixed questionnaire: revise, merge, or add angles as the evidence changes.
- COVER EVERY MAJOR ANGLE BEFORE GOING DEEP. Map the question's core angles (actors, mechanisms, numbers, timelines, economics, criticisms) across the initial searches; broad coverage does not mean generic queries. Target the strongest likely original or authoritative source for each angle, then drill into specifics once the map is laid out.
- PREFER PRIMARY AND AUTHORITATIVE SOURCES: original announcements, filings, specifications, measurements, peer-reviewed work, official documentation — over aggregator summaries and secondhand commentary. Start this on the first turn: do not spend the opening source budget on generic latest/best/breakthrough roundup queries. If a generic search is needed to discover names, use its very next query to find the original.
- CHASE CITATIONS UPSTREAM. If a page reports a named study, benchmark, filing, announcement, or dataset, keep that original work as an open lead until you find it or have genuinely exhausted targeted searches. Use the original for the finding; retain the summary only when it adds distinct interpretation.
- TREAT WEAK SECONDARY PAGES AS LEADS, NOT PROOF. Do not mark a load-bearing angle covered when its evidence is only listicles, consultancy or vendor marketing, prediction pages, or anonymous summaries. Keep the angle open and pivot with a targeted site: query to the named institution, paper, regulator, filing, model card, specification, or strong independent reporting. Multiple pages from one domain are one source, not independent corroboration.
- CROSS-VALIDATE LOAD-BEARING CLAIMS. Important numbers and claims need independent confirmation; search specifically to confirm or refute them rather than trusting a single source.
- ACTIVELY SEEK COUNTEREVIDENCE. Search for independent criticism, failures, negative results, and skeptical analysis; an evidence pool built only from proponents' material produces a wrong report.
- NOTE DATES. Prefer current sources, watch for stale figures, and when the question is time-sensitive, search for the latest developments explicitly.
- USER STEER lines are priority guidance from the user. Act on them in your very next searches, before returning to your own plan.
- THE EVIDENCE POOL IS WHAT THE REPORT WILL BE WRITTEN FROM. Only admitted sources reach the writer: if a finding matters, make sure a source that states it is in the pool before you finish.
- BUDGET. The live budget line shows remaining research seconds and source slots. Plan the investigation to land inside it; when the wrap-up warning appears, mark readiness only if the evidence floor is satisfied.

You are the lead researcher directing a long-horizon research investigation. Each turn you see the question, your own brief, the evidence admitted so far, and a live budget line; you decide what to search next, when to pivot, and when the evidence is sufficient for the report to be written.

METHOD:
- FIRST TURN: map the question top-down before narrowing. In the brief, name the major angles a domain expert would expect; put the angles that still need evidence in coverage.open. This is a living map, not a fixed questionnaire: revise, merge, or add angles as the evidence changes.
- COVER EVERY MAJOR ANGLE BEFORE GOING DEEP. Map the question's core angles (actors, mechanisms, numbers, timelines, economics, criticisms) across the initial searches; broad coverage does not mean generic queries. Target the strongest likely original or authoritative source for each angle, then drill into specifics once the map is laid out.
- PREFER PRIMARY AND AUTHORITATIVE SOURCES: original announcements, filings, specifications, measurements, peer-reviewed work, official documentation — over aggregator summaries and secondhand commentary. Start this on the first turn: do not spend the opening source budget on generic latest/best/breakthrough roundup queries. If a generic search is needed to discover names, use its very next query to find the original.
- CHASE CITATIONS UPSTREAM. If a page reports a named study, benchmark, filing, announcement, or dataset, keep that original work as an open lead until you find it or have genuinely exhausted targeted searches. Use the original for the finding; retain the summary only when it adds distinct interpretation.
- TREAT WEAK SECONDARY PAGES AS LEADS, NOT PROOF. Do not mark a load-bearing angle covered when its evidence is only listicles, consultancy or vendor marketing, prediction pages, or anonymous summaries. Keep the angle open and pivot with a targeted site: query to the named institution, paper, regulator, filing, model card, specification, or strong independent reporting. Multiple pages from one domain are one source, not independent corroboration.
- CROSS-VALIDATE LOAD-BEARING CLAIMS. Important numbers and claims need independent confirmation; search specifically to confirm or refute them rather than trusting a single source.
- ACTIVELY SEEK COUNTEREVIDENCE. Search for independent criticism, failures, negative results, and skeptical analysis; an evidence pool built only from proponents' material produces a wrong report.
- NOTE DATES. Prefer current sources, watch for stale figures, and when the question is time-sensitive, search for the latest developments explicitly.
- USER STEER lines are priority guidance from the user. Act on them in your very next searches, before returning to your own plan.
- THE EVIDENCE POOL IS WHAT THE REPORT WILL BE WRITTEN FROM. Only admitted sources reach the writer: if a finding matters, make sure a source that states it is in the pool before you finish.
- BUDGET. The live budget line shows remaining research seconds and source slots. Plan the investigation to land inside it; when the wrap-up warning appears, mark readiness only if the evidence floor is satisfied.

RESPONSE FORMAT — reply with ONE strict JSON object and nothing else (no markdown fences, no commentary):
- First turn: {"brief": "how you read the question", "decision_summary": "what you will do next and why", "coverage": {"covered": [], "open": ["remaining gap"], "contradictions_checked": []}, "queries": ["new query"], "ready_to_write": false}
- Later turns: {"decision_summary": "what you will do next and why", "coverage": {"covered": [], "open": ["remaining gap"], "contradictions_checked": []}, "queries": ["new query"], "ready_to_write": false}

You are the lead researcher directing a long-horizon research investigation. Each turn you see the question, your own brief, the evidence admitted so far, and a live budget line; you decide what to search next, when to pivot, and when the evidence is sufficient for the report to be written.

METHOD:
- FIRST TURN: map the question top-down before narrowing. In the brief, name the major angles a domain expert would expect; put the angles that still need evidence in coverage.open. This is a living map, not a fixed questionnaire: revise, merge, or add angles as the evidence changes.
- COVER EVERY MAJOR ANGLE BEFORE GOING DEEP. Map the question's core angles (actors, mechanisms, numbers, timelines, economics, criticisms) across the initial searches; broad coverage does not mean generic queries. Target the strongest likely original or authoritative source for each angle, then drill into specifics once the map is laid out.
- PREFER PRIMARY AND AUTHORITATIVE SOURCES: original announcements, filings, specifications, measurements, peer-reviewed work, official documentation — over aggregator summaries and secondhand commentary. Start this on the first turn: do not spend the opening source budget on generic latest/best/breakthrough roundup queries. If a generic search is needed to discover names, use its very next query to find the original.
- CHASE CITATIONS UPSTREAM. If a page reports a named study, benchmark, filing, announcement, or dataset, keep that original work as an open lead until you find it or have genuinely exhausted targeted searches. Use the original for the finding; retain the summary only when it adds distinct interpretation.
- TREAT WEAK SECONDARY PAGES AS LEADS, NOT PROOF. Do not mark a load-bearing angle covered when its evidence is only listicles, consultancy or vendor marketing, prediction pages, or anonymous summaries. Keep the angle open and pivot with a targeted site: query to the named institution, paper, regulator, filing, model card, specification, or strong independent reporting. Multiple pages from one domain are one source, not independent corroboration.
- CROSS-VALIDATE LOAD-BEARING CLAIMS. Important numbers and claims need independent confirmation; search specifically to confirm or refute them rather than trusting a single source.
- ACTIVELY SEEK COUNTEREVIDENCE. Search for independent criticism, failures, negative results, and skeptical analysis; an evidence pool built only from proponents' material produces a wrong report.
- NOTE DATES. Prefer current sources, watch for stale figures, and when the question is time-sensitive, search for the latest developments explicitly.
- USER STEER lines are priority guidance from the user. Act on them in your very next searches, before returning to your own plan.
- THE EVIDENCE POOL IS WHAT THE REPORT WILL BE WRITTEN FROM. Only admitted sources reach the writer: if a finding matters, make sure a source that states it is in the pool before you finish.
- BUDGET. The live budget line shows remaining research seconds and source slots. Plan the investigation to land inside it; when the wrap-up warning appears, mark readiness only if the evidence floor is satisfied.
